newsitem.title: USA: US, EU negotiators tackle meat dispute again.
newsitem.headline: US, EU negotiators tackle meat dispute again.

text.p: U.S. and EU officials were scheduled to meet Friday afternoon to continue what has so far been fruitless attempts to resolve a bitter dispute over meat and poultry import inspection regulations.

The prevalent feeling among U.S. industry sources was that it looked doubtful that any agreement would be reached by day's end, and some speculation persisted that the talks may continue next week in Brussels.
Agriculture Department officials briefed U.S. industry representatives on Thursday afternoon and Friday morning on the state of the talks and the EU's latest proposal.

The talks remain deadlocked on the poultry decontamination issue. The talks had been scheduled expected to end Thursday, with or without an agreement. EU officials decided mid-day to remain in Washington for one more day of talks.

On Thursday, the EU offered to do a scientific review of the use of decontaminants in poultry plants, but said the plan would only study the use of lactic acid and TSP in the process, not chlorine, which is the bacteria-fighting agent used by the U.S. industry.
U.S. officials said they were taking the proposal under serious consideration, but that they were concerned about the EU's refusal to consider chlorine as a decontaminant.

Industry sources said that despite some progress in several disputed areas as long as the various issues are being considered in an "all or nothing" package, it will make it difficult to reach a successful conclusion.

"This is a major problem on poultry, and I don't know how they're going to deal with it," said an official with the American Meat Institute. "The EU is holding the rest of the deal hostage for poultry."

U.S. and EU officials have been meeting in Washington since Tuesday to try to work out a deal in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks. Failure to reach an agreement could halt hundreds of millions of dollars of trans-Atlantic meat and poultry trade.

Since April 1, U.S. poultry shipments potentially worth some $50 million have been halted to Europe due to new EU inspection rules. And as of April 15, up to $300 million worth of EU meat exports to the United States may be disrupted because of new U.S. regulations.

Officials have been working to reach a deal by the April 15 deadline to avoid a further escalation of the dispute. EU officials have threatened "quick and decisive" action if the United States restricts imports of EU meat, but U.S. officials said Thursday that extending the April 15 deadline "is not a possibility."
